questions.question: Which of the following is part of Arrhenius's theory of acids and bases?
questions.answer: **A.** Arrhenius defined an acid as a substance that produces $\text{H}^+$ in water and a base as one that produces $\text{OH}^-$ in water.
options: Acidity is due to the presence of oxygen in non-metal compounds.
Compounds which contain hydrogen are acidic in nature.

questions.question: Which class of organic molecules undergoes addition reactions?
questions.answer: **A.** The C=C double bond of an alkene can open to add atoms across it.

questions.question: A solution of HCl(aq) has a pH of 2 and an equimolar solution of acid X has a pH of 1.8. Acid X is most likely to be a:
questions.answer: **B.** At $0.010\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$, X gives $[\text{H}^+]=10^{-1.8}=0.016\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$, more than one $\text{H}^+$ per molecule, so it donates more than one proton and does so extensively.

questions.question: In which of the following reactions would decreasing the volume of the reaction vessel (at constant temperature) leave the amounts of reactants and products unchanged?
questions.answer: **D.** There are 2 mol of gas on each side, so a change in volume does not favour either direction.

questions.question: Which of the molecules shown is a secondary amide?
questions.answer: **B.** A secondary amide has one H and one alkyl group on the nitrogen besides the carbonyl carbon (here N-methylpropanamide). A and D are tertiary and C is primary.

questions.question:
Consider the titration apparatus shown. Which combination of liquids should be used to rinse the glassware before the titration to improve its accuracy?

(Each option lists burette / pipette / conical flask.)
questions.answer: **C.** The burette and pipette are rinsed with the solutions they will deliver so those solutions are not diluted. The flask is rinsed with water, which does not change the moles of analyte placed in it.
options: deionised water / deionised water / deionised water

questions.question: In which of the following titrations would buffering of the solution occur?
questions.answer: **B.** Part-way through, the flask contains significant amounts of both the weak base and its conjugate acid.
options: A strong acid added to a strong base
A strong acid added to a weak base
A strong base added to a strong acid
A weak acid added to water

questions.question: Which of the following molecules will **not** react with acidified potassium dichromate solution?
questions.answer: **A.** 2-methylbutan-2-ol is a tertiary alcohol: the carbon bearing the OH has no hydrogen, so it is not oxidised.

questions.question: Which of the following is true for 3-methylbutan-2-one, shown below?
questions.answer: **C.** Adding water across the triple bond (OH to the more substituted carbon) gives an enol that rearranges to the ketone. Ketones do not reduce Tollens' reagent, it is not an isomer of $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{12}\text{O}$, and it has only four carbon environments.
options: It forms a silver mirror on treatment with Tollens' reagent $[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$.
It is a functional group isomer of pentan-1-ol.
It may be prepared by the catalysed hydration of 3-methylbut-1-yne.
It will show five distinct carbon atoms in spectroscopy.

questions.question: A 35 mL sample of 0.25 mol L$^{-1}$ NaOH solution was placed in a 1 L volumetric flask and filled to the mark with deionised water. What is the pH of the final solution?
Methane reacts with an **excess** of chlorine in the presence of UV light. What are the products if the reaction goes to completion?
questions.answer: **D.** Free-radical substitution continues until all four H atoms are replaced: $\text{CH}_4+4\text{Cl}_2\rightarrow\text{CCl}_4+4\text{HCl}$.

questions.question: What is the IUPAC name for the compound shown?
questions.answer: **C.** Number the heptane chain to give the lowest locants (2,2,3,4) and list the prefixes alphabetically: chloro, fluoro, methyl.

questions.question: Which compound would have the ${}^{13}$C NMR spectrum shown?
questions.answer: **B.** There are five signals, one near 200 ppm, which is the C=O of an aldehyde or ketone (an acid appears at 160–185 ppm).

questions.question: Equal amounts of four compounds are added to the same volume of water. Which produces the solution with the highest pH?
questions.answer: **D.** Ethanamine is a base. The amide and ester are essentially neutral and ethanoic acid is acidic.

questions.question:
$$2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)$$

One mole of sulfur dioxide and two moles of oxygen are mixed in a reaction vessel and allowed to proceed towards equilibrium. Which statement about this system is true?
questions.answer: **D.** By stoichiometry, 1 mol of $\text{O}_2$ is used for every 2 mol of $\text{SO}_3$ formed.
options: $[\text{SO}_2]$ will increase at the same rate as $[\text{SO}_3]$.
$[\text{O}_2]$ will decrease at double the rate that $[\text{SO}_2]$ is decreasing.
$[\text{O}_2]$ will decrease at half the rate that $[\text{SO}_3]$ is increasing.

questions.question: The $K_{sp}$ of chromium(III) hydroxide is $6.3\times10^{-31}$. What is the concentration (mol L$^{-1}$) of chromium(III) ions in a saturated solution of chromium(III) hydroxide?
questions.answer:
**C.** $K_{sp}=[\text{Cr}^{3+}][\text{OH}^-]^3=s(3s)^3=27s^4$.

*Note: this intended calculation ignores the $\text{OH}^-$ from water itself, which for so insoluble a hydroxide would actually lower $[\text{Cr}^{3+}]$ further.*

questions.question: 1 mL of an acid with a pH of 5 is added to 999 mL of deionised water. What is the pH of the new solution?
questions.answer: **C.** The acid contributes only $10^{-8}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ of $\text{H}^+$, far less than water's $10^{-7}$, so the pH is just under 7. An acid cannot become basic on dilution.

questions.question:
Which compound has the highest solubility (in g L$^{-1}$)?

| Compound | Molar mass (g mol$^{-1}$) | $K_{sp}$ |
|---|---|---|
| Lithium chloride | 42.39 | 395 |
| Sodium chloride | 58.44 | 42 |
| Potassium chloride | 74.55 | 22 |
| Rubidium chloride | 120.9 | 56 |
questions.answer: **D.** Solubility $=\sqrt{K_{sp}}\times M$: LiCl 842, NaCl 379, KCl 350, RbCl 905 g L$^{-1}$.

questions.question:
$$\text{H}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons2\text{HI}(g)\qquad\Delta H=-9.5\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

Which change, imposed on this system at equilibrium, will result in an increased concentration of HI(g) when equilibrium is re-established?
questions.answer: **A.** Halving the volume doubles both gas concentrations, so $Q=[\text{HI}]^2/[\text{H}_2]$ doubles and the system shifts left only until $Q=K$. The final $[\text{HI}]$ is still higher than before. Adding solid has no effect, removing HI lowers it, and heating an exothermic reaction lowers it.
options: Halving the volume of the system
Increasing the temperature of the system

questions.question:
$$\text{W}(g)+2\text{X}(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{Y}(g)+\text{Z}(g)\qquad K_c=200$$

0.5 mol of W and 0.5 mol of X are placed in a sealed 0.5 L vessel and allowed to react. Which is true once the system reaches equilibrium?
questions.answer: **B.** Both start at $1.0\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ but X is used twice as fast as W, so less X remains.

questions.question: State the Brønsted–Lowry definition of a base.
questions.answer: A Brønsted–Lowry base is a proton ($\text{H}^+$) acceptor.

questions.question: Explain how the Brønsted–Lowry definition of a base is an improvement on the Arrhenius model, using an example and a relevant equation to illustrate this.
questions.answer:
Arrhenius defined a base as a substance that releases $\text{OH}^-$ ions in water. This cannot account for substances that behave as bases but contain no hydroxide, or for reactions that do not occur in water.

Brønsted and Lowry defined a base as a proton acceptor, which is independent of hydroxide and of the solvent. For example, ammonia contains no OH group but neutralises hydrogen chloride:
$$\text{NH}_3(g)+\text{HCl}(g)\rightarrow\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}(s)$$
$\text{NH}_3$ accepts a proton from HCl, so it is a Brønsted–Lowry base, even though no water or $\text{OH}^-$ is involved.

questions.question: Identify a limitation of the Brønsted–Lowry model.
questions.answer: It cannot explain acid–base reactions that involve no proton transfer, such as an acidic oxide reacting with a basic oxide ($\text{CaO}+\text{SiO}_2\rightarrow\text{CaSiO}_3$), or $\text{BF}_3$ reacting with $\text{NH}_3$.

questions.question: The $K_{sp}$ for barium fluoride is $3.10\times10^{-6}$. Calculate the solubility (in g per 100 mL) of barium fluoride.
questions.answer:
$\text{BaF}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ba}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{F}^-(aq)$, so $K_{sp}=s(2s)^2=4s^3$.
$$s=\sqrt[3]{\frac{3.10\times10^{-6}}{4}}=9.19\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$
Molar mass $=175.3\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, so solubility $=1.61\ \text{g L}^{-1}=0.161$ g per 100 mL.

questions.question: A piece of equipment often used in a titration is shown. Name it and identify its purpose in a titration.
questions.answer: It is a **volumetric (bulb) pipette**. It is used to transfer an accurately known volume (aliquot) of one solution, usually into the conical flask.

questions.question:
The titration curve shows the change in pH when a 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ monoprotic strong acid is added incrementally to a strong base.

Sketch the curve you would get if a 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ monoprotic **weak** acid were added incrementally to the same base solution.

Indicators used in titrations are usually weak acids. In a titration in which a strong acid is added from the burette to a strong base in the flask, identify and explain the effect of adding too much indicator.
questions.answer:
**Effect:** the titre of acid is too low, so the calculated concentration of the base is lower than the true value.

**Explanation:** the indicator is itself a weak acid, so a large amount of it neutralises a significant part of the base. Less acid from the burette is then needed to reach the end point.

questions.question:
Dinitrogen tetroxide, a colourless gas, decomposes to form brown nitrogen dioxide gas:
$$\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)\qquad\Delta H=+57\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

A mixture of the two gases is placed in a sealed syringe. Using collision theory, explain the effect of increasing the temperature of this system on the equilibrium constant, $K_c$.
questions.answer:
Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the molecules, so they collide more often and, more importantly, a larger fraction of collisions have energy of at least the activation energy. The rates of **both** forward and reverse reactions increase.

The forward reaction is endothermic, so it has the larger activation energy. The fraction of successful collisions therefore increases proportionally more for the forward reaction, and the forward rate exceeds the reverse rate.

The system shifts right until the rates are equal again, with more $\text{NO}_2$ and less $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$.

Since $K_c=\dfrac{[\text{NO}_2]^2}{[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]}$, **$K_c$ increases**.

questions.question:
Dinitrogen tetroxide, a colourless gas, decomposes to form brown nitrogen dioxide gas:
$$\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)\qquad\Delta H=+57\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

A 1.00 L reaction vessel containing 0.100 mol of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ gas is allowed to come to equilibrium. 0.250 mol of $\text{NO}_2$ is then added and the system allowed to reach equilibrium again. The final concentration of $\text{NO}_2$ is 0.400 mol L$^{-1}$. The temperature is constant throughout. Calculate $K_c$ for this reaction.
questions.answer:
The final equilibrium is the same as if all the substances had been present at the start:

| | $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ | $\text{NO}_2$ |
|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0.100 | 0.250 |
| Change | $-x$ | $+2x$ |
| Equilibrium | $0.100-x$ | 0.400 |

$0.250+2x=0.400$, so $x=0.075$ and $[\text{N}_2\text{O}_4]=0.025$.
$$K_c=\frac{0.400^2}{0.025}=6.4$$

questions.question: Vitamins are biologically important molecules. The structures of vitamins A and C are shown. Vitamin A is fat soluble whereas vitamin C is water soluble. Account for the difference in their solubilities.
questions.answer:
**Vitamin A** is a large, mostly non-polar hydrocarbon with only one hydroxyl group. Its main intermolecular forces are dispersion forces, which are similar to those between fat molecules, so it dissolves readily in fat. In water, the single OH group cannot offset the large hydrocarbon part, which would disrupt many hydrogen bonds between water molecules without forming comparable attractions.

**Vitamin C** is a small molecule with several hydroxyl groups and a carbonyl group. It is very polar and forms many hydrogen bonds with water, releasing enough energy to compensate for breaking the hydrogen bonds in water and between vitamin C molecules, so it is water soluble. It cannot form strong attractions with non-polar fat molecules.

*Note: the paper's drawing of vitamin C omits the ring oxygen (ascorbic acid is a cyclic ester), but the argument is unaffected.*

questions.question:
The table shows some structural isomers with the molecular formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$.

Give the structure of a position isomer of isomer A.
questions.answer: **Pent-1-ene**, $\text{CH}_2\text{=CHCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ (A is pent-2-ene; only the position of the double bond differs).

questions.question:
The table shows some structural isomers with the molecular formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$.

Identify a suitable chemical test to distinguish between samples of isomer A and isomer B, stating the expected results.
questions.answer:
Add **bromine water** (without UV light) to each and shake.

- Isomer A (an alkene) decolourises it quickly: orange-brown to colourless, by addition across the C=C.
- Isomer B (cyclopentane) does not react, so the orange-brown colour remains.

questions.question:
The table shows some structural isomers with the molecular formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$.

Name isomer C.
questions.answer: **2-methylbut-2-ene**

questions.question:
The table shows some structural isomers with the molecular formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}$.

Give the structures of the product(s) formed when isomer C is hydrated using dilute sulfuric acid.

Gaseous A molecules undergo a reversible reaction to form gaseous B molecules. The graph shows how the concentrations of A(g) and B(g) change over time in a 2.0 L vessel at constant temperature (the graph for A is not completed).

Explain the shape of the [B] curve from 0 to 8 min.
questions.answer:
At the start there is no B, so only the forward reaction occurs and it is at its fastest because $[\text{A}]$ is greatest: $[\text{B}]$ rises steeply.

As A is used up, collisions between A particles become less frequent and the forward rate falls; as B builds up, the reverse rate rises. $[\text{B}]$ therefore increases more and more slowly.

From about 6 min the forward and reverse rates are equal. The system is at dynamic equilibrium and $[\text{B}]$ stays constant at $0.60\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.

questions.question:
Gaseous A molecules undergo a reversible reaction to form gaseous B molecules. The graph shows how the concentrations of A(g) and B(g) change over time in a 2.0 L vessel at constant temperature (the graph for A is not completed).

Calculate the equilibrium constant for this system.
questions.answer:
From the graph $[\text{A}]$ falls by 0.20 while $[\text{B}]$ rises by 0.60, so the reaction is $\text{A}(g)\rightleftharpoons3\text{B}(g)$.
$$K=\frac{[\text{B}]^3}{[\text{A}]}=\frac{0.60^3}{0.80}=0.27$$

questions.question:
Gaseous A molecules undergo a reversible reaction to form gaseous B molecules. The graph shows how the concentrations of A(g) and B(g) change over time in a 2.0 L vessel at constant temperature (the graph for A is not completed).

At 8 min some A(g) is added to the 2.0 L vessel. Calculate the amount (in mol) of A(g) added.
questions.answer:
From the first equilibrium, $\text{A}\rightleftharpoons3\text{B}$ with $K=0.60^3/0.80=0.27$.

At the new equilibrium $[\text{B}]=0.90$, so
$$[\text{A}]=\frac{0.90^3}{0.27}=2.7\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

B increased by 0.30, so 0.10 mol L$^{-1}$ of A reacted after the addition. If $y$ mol L$^{-1}$ of A was added:
$$0.80+y-0.10=2.7\Rightarrow y=2.0\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$
Amount added $=2.0\times2.0=4.0$ mol.

questions.question: The p$K_a$ of methanoic acid is 3.75. Determine the pH of a 2.0 mol L$^{-1}$ solution.
questions.answer:
$K_a=10^{-3.75}=1.78\times10^{-4}$.

For $\text{HA}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{H}_3\text{O}^++\text{A}^-$, assuming $x\ll2.0$:
$$K_a=\frac{x^2}{2.0}\Rightarrow x=\sqrt{1.78\times10^{-4}\times2.0}=0.0189\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$
(under 1% of 2.0, so the assumption holds).
$$\text{pH}=-\log_{10}(0.0189)=1.72$$

questions.question: When 100 mL of 0.500 mol L$^{-1}$ copper(II) nitrate solution is added to 150 mL of 0.800 mol L$^{-1}$ potassium hydroxide solution, a precipitate is produced. Calculate the concentrations of copper(II) ions and hydroxide ions remaining in solution after precipitation.
questions.answer:
$\text{Cu}^{2+}+2\text{OH}^-\rightarrow\text{Cu(OH)}_2(s)$

$n(\text{Cu}^{2+})=0.0500$ mol and $n(\text{OH}^-)=0.120$ mol. $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ is limiting and uses 0.100 mol of $\text{OH}^-$.

$$[\text{OH}^-]=\frac{0.020}{0.250}=0.080\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

The small amount of copper(II) left in solution is set by $K_{sp}=2.2\times10^{-20}$:
$$[\text{Cu}^{2+}]=\frac{2.2\times10^{-20}}{0.080^2}=3.4\times10^{-18}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$$

questions.question:
Ethyl benzoate has a pleasant odour described as cherry and grape. It can be synthesised from benzaldehyde via an intermediate A, as shown in the diagram.

Give: (i) the structure of intermediate A, (ii) the reagent for Step 1, (iii) the structure of the other reactant in Step 2, and (iv) the conditions for Step 2.
questions.answer:
1. Intermediate A: **benzoic acid**, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$.
2. Step 1: an oxidant, e.g. acidified potassium permanganate ($\text{MnO}_4^-/\text{H}^+$) or acidified dichromate.
3. Other reactant: **ethanol**, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$.
4. Conditions: concentrated sulfuric acid catalyst, heat under reflux.

questions.question:
Ethyl benzoate has a pleasant odour described as cherry and grape. It can be synthesised from benzaldehyde via an intermediate A, as shown in the diagram.

Identify a **chemical** test, including the predicted results, that can distinguish between ethyl benzoate and benzaldehyde.
questions.answer:
**Tollens' test:** warm each with Tollens' reagent, $[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$. Benzaldehyde is oxidised and a silver mirror (or grey-black silver precipitate) forms; ethyl benzoate gives no change.

(2,4-dinitrophenylhydrazine also works: an orange precipitate with benzaldehyde only.)

questions.question:
The enthalpy of neutralisation when sodium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid is $-57.3$ kJ per mole of water formed.

Write the net ionic equation for this neutralisation reaction, including details of $\Delta H$.
questions.answer: $$\text{H}^+(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\qquad\Delta H=-57.3\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$$

questions.question:
The enthalpy of neutralisation when sodium hydroxide reacts with sulfuric acid is $-57.3$ kJ per mole of water formed.

110.0 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide (density 1.04 g mL$^{-1}$) is mixed with 50.0 mL of 1.00 mol L$^{-1}$ sulfuric acid (density 1.06 g mL$^{-1}$) in a styrofoam cup. Each solution is initially at 25.0 °C. Assuming the resulting solution has a specific heat capacity of 3.93 J K$^{-1}$ g$^{-1}$, calculate the final temperature reached.
questions.answer:
$\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4+2\text{NaOH}\rightarrow\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4+2\text{H}_2\text{O}$

$n(\text{NaOH})=0.110$ mol, $n(\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4)=0.0500$ mol, so the acid is limiting and $n(\text{H}_2\text{O})=0.100$ mol.

Heat released: $q=0.100\times57.3\ \text{kJ}=5730$ J.

Mass of solution: $110.0\times1.04+50.0\times1.06=167.4$ g.
$$\Delta T=\frac{q}{mc}=\frac{5730}{167.4\times3.93}=8.71\ \text{K}$$
Final temperature $=25.0+8.71=33.7$ °C.

questions.question: Polyisoprene, used in some golf balls, is an addition polymer. Its monomer, isoprene, is a **branched**, non-cyclic hydrocarbon that is 88.16% carbon by mass. Its mass spectrum is shown. Give a possible structure for isoprene, showing all working.
questions.answer:
The molecular ion is at $m/z=68$, so $M=68$.

Mass of carbon: $0.8816\times68=60$, i.e. 5 C atoms. The remaining $68-60=8$ gives 8 H atoms: $\text{C}_5\text{H}_8$.

A branched, non-cyclic structure that can polymerise by addition is **2-methylbuta-1,3-diene**:
$$\text{CH}_2\text{=C(CH}_3)\text{-CH=CH}_2$$

(3-methylbut-1-yne also fits the data given.)

questions.question: Polyurethane is a condensation polymer. Describe one difference between an addition polymer and a condensation polymer.
questions.answer: When a condensation polymer forms, a small molecule (such as water) is released at each link, whereas in addition polymerisation the monomers join with no by-product, so the polymer contains every atom of the monomers.

questions.question: The repeating unit of a polyurethane is shown. Give the structures of possible monomers that could be combined to synthesise it.
questions.answer:
**Ethane-1,2-diol**, $\text{HOCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$, and **ethane-1,2-diisocyanate**, $\text{O=C=N-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-N=C=O}$.

(A condensation-style pair such as ethane-1,2-diamine with $\text{HOOC-O-CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{-O-COOH}$ is also accepted on paper.)

*Note: industrially polyurethanes are made from a diol and a diisocyanate, which join without releasing a small molecule, although the paper classes polyurethane as a condensation polymer.*

questions.question: 12 mL of calcium hydroxide solution (pH = 11.5) is mixed with 7.0 mL of nitric acid (pH = 1.8). Calculate the final pH of the solution.
questions.answer:
$[\text{OH}^-]=10^{-(14-11.5)}=3.16\times10^{-3}$, so $n(\text{OH}^-)=3.16\times10^{-3}\times0.012=3.79\times10^{-5}$ mol.

$[\text{H}^+]=10^{-1.8}=0.01585$, so $n(\text{H}^+)=0.01585\times0.0070=1.11\times10^{-4}$ mol.

$\text{H}^++\text{OH}^-\rightarrow\text{H}_2\text{O}$, so excess $n(\text{H}^+)=7.30\times10^{-5}$ mol.
$$[\text{H}^+]=\frac{7.30\times10^{-5}}{0.019}=3.84\times10^{-3}\ \text{mol L}^{-1},\qquad\text{pH}=2.42$$
(The pH of the calcium hydroxide already accounts for both of its hydroxide ions.)

questions.question: Consider the reaction scheme shown. Outline the reagents and conditions for each step, then discuss whether you could use the features shown in both infrared (IR) and proton NMR spectroscopy to confirm that each product has been formed from its reactant.
questions.answer:
**Step 1: ethane (A) → chloroethane (B).** Reagent $\text{Cl}_2$ with UV light (free-radical substitution).

- IR: of **limited use**. Both show C–H and C–C absorptions. The C–Cl absorption lies in the crowded fingerprint region (about 600–800 cm$^{-1}$), so B is hard to identify except by matching a reference spectrum.
- ¹H NMR: **very useful**. Ethane gives a single singlet (six equivalent H). Chloroethane gives two signals, a triplet (3H) and a quartet (2H) further downfield, ratio 3:2.

**Step 2: chloroethane → ethanol (C).** Reagent dilute NaOH or KOH(aq), heat (substitution).

- IR: **very useful**. A new broad O–H absorption appears at 3230–3550 cm$^{-1}$.
- ¹H NMR: **useful**. There are now three signals: a triplet (3H), a quartet (2H) and a singlet (1H, the O–H), ratio 3:2:1. The CH$_3$/CH$_2$ pattern resembles B's, so the new O–H signal and the shift of the CH$_2$ are the evidence.

**Step 3: ethanol → ethanal (D).** Reagent a mild oxidant such as PCC, or acidified dichromate with the ethanal distilled off as it forms so it is not oxidised further.

- IR: **very useful**. The broad O–H absorption disappears and a strong, sharp C=O absorption appears at 1680–1750 cm$^{-1}$ (and no very broad acid O–H at 2500–3000 cm$^{-1}$ shows it has not become ethanoic acid).
- ¹H NMR: **very useful**. There are two signals in ratio 3:1: a doublet (CH$_3$) and a quartet (CHO) far downfield at about 9.5–10 ppm.

**Judgement.** ¹H NMR can confirm every product. IR is decisive when a functional group with a distinctive absorption appears or disappears (steps 2 and 3) but not for step 1.

*Note: the school's table says ethanal normally shows two singlets. The CHO and CH$_3$ protons do split each other (quartet and doublet), and this is what should be expected in an exam answer.*

questions.question:
Three unknown 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ solutions each contain one cation and one anion from:

- cations: $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, $\text{Na}^+$, $\text{Ag}^+$, $\text{Pb}^{2+}$
- anions: $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$, $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$, $\text{Cl}^-$

Tests on fresh samples gave these results (NVR = no visible reaction):

| Test | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Add $\text{HNO}_3(aq)$ | bubbles | vinegar smell | NVR |
| Add $\text{BaCl}_2(aq)$ | white precipitate | white precipitate that darkened in UV | NVR |
| Add $\text{NH}_3(aq)$ or $\text{OH}^-(aq)$ | NVR | brown precipitate that dissolved in excess ammonia | white precipitate |

Determine the chemical formulae of samples A–C.
questions.answer:
- **A: $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$.** Bubbles with acid show carbonate; BaCl$_2$ gives $\text{BaCO}_3$; no precipitate with base means $\text{Na}^+$.
- **B: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOAg}$.** Vinegar smell shows ethanoate; with BaCl$_2$ the chloride precipitates white AgCl, which darkens in light; the brown precipitate is $\text{Ag}_2\text{O}$.
- **C: $\text{MgCl}_2$.** No reaction with acid or $\text{Ba}^{2+}$ rules out carbonate, sulfate and (no smell) ethanoate, leaving chloride; the white precipitate with base is then $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ ($\text{Pb}^{2+}$ is ruled out because it could not stay dissolved with chloride at this concentration).

*Note: silver ethanoate is only soluble to about 0.06 mol L$^{-1}$ at room temperature, so a 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ solution of B is not really possible.*

questions.question:
Three unknown 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ solutions each contain one cation and one anion from:

- cations: $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, $\text{Na}^+$, $\text{Ag}^+$, $\text{Pb}^{2+}$
- anions: $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$, $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$, $\text{Cl}^-$

Tests on fresh samples gave these results (NVR = no visible reaction):

| Test | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Add $\text{HNO}_3(aq)$ | bubbles | vinegar smell | NVR |
| Add $\text{BaCl}_2(aq)$ | white precipitate | white precipitate that darkened in UV | NVR |
| Add $\text{NH}_3(aq)$ or $\text{OH}^-(aq)$ | NVR | brown precipitate that dissolved in excess ammonia | white precipitate |

Outline why the brown precipitate dissolved in excess ammonia for solution B.
questions.answer: Ammonia forms the soluble complex ion $[\text{Ag(NH}_3)_2]^+$. This lowers the concentration of free $\text{Ag}^+$, so the precipitate dissolves.

questions.question:
Three unknown 0.1 mol L$^{-1}$ solutions each contain one cation and one anion from:

- cations: $\text{Mg}^{2+}$, $\text{Na}^+$, $\text{Ag}^+$, $\text{Pb}^{2+}$
- anions: $\text{CO}_3^{2-}$, $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$, $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$, $\text{Cl}^-$

Tests on fresh samples gave these results (NVR = no visible reaction):

| Test | A | B | C |
|---|---|---|---|
| Add $\text{HNO}_3(aq)$ | bubbles | vinegar smell | NVR |
| Add $\text{BaCl}_2(aq)$ | white precipitate | white precipitate that darkened in UV | NVR |
| Add $\text{NH}_3(aq)$ or $\text{OH}^-(aq)$ | NVR | brown precipitate that dissolved in excess ammonia | white precipitate |

Identify why you would need to monitor the environment for any one of these ions.
questions.answer: $\text{Pb}^{2+}$ is toxic to humans and aquatic life even at very low concentrations and accumulates in organisms, so water and soil must be checked to ensure levels stay within safe limits.
